passage:
Arnab, sulking because the guests finished the fish fry? Sit. Let your Lavanya Paati tell you about the payasam.

When I was ten, in Thanjavur, important guests came to see my elder sister. Amma made me wear my stiff silk skirt, sit on the mat with my knees together, and not say one word. Guests ate first, of course.

I watched them finish the whole vessel of payasam. My favourite. I smiled on the outside and burned on the inside.

After they left, I cried to Appa that the house was a stage and I was a doll on it.

He didn't scold. He scraped the vessel and gave me the last spoonful. "Outside face for guests, inside face for us," he said. "Both are true. Now eat."

qa.q: What did the guests finish?
qa.a: They finished the whole vessel of payasam.

qa.q: What was young Lavanya feeling as she watched the guests eat?
qa.a: She felt resentful and hurt, smiling on the outside while burning inside at losing her favourite dish.

qa.q: What turning point helped young Lavanya accept the guest rules?
qa.a: Appa didn't scold her; he gave her the last spoonful and explained that the house has an outside face and an inside face, both true.

qa.q: How might Appa have seen Lavanya's tears?
qa.a: Appa saw a child who had held herself together all evening, and wanted to comfort her rather than punish her.

grounding: Shows a child told to sit properly and let guests eat first, resenting the lost favourite dish and learning that home has a public and a private face.

passage:
Monsoon rain kept Manjula Aunty and her three children stuck in the one-room flat in Pune for the whole evening.

"Sit properly, Sharmila," Aai whispered. "No sprawling. And guests first."

So Sharmila sat on the edge of the bed with her feet together, smiling politely, while the cousins ate the gulab jamuns she had helped fry that morning. One, two, three. Gone. She had been saving one in her mind all day.

She said "Yes, Aunty" and "No, Aunty" and nothing else for three hours.

When the rain stopped and the door closed behind them, Aai flopped onto the bed. Baba loosened his collar. Everybody laughed at once.

Then Aai opened the steel box on top of the fridge. Two gulab jamuns, hidden. "For the best-behaved girl in Pune."

qa.q: For how long did Sharmila say only 'Yes, Aunty' and 'No, Aunty'?
qa.a: For three hours.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling as the cousins ate the gulab jamuns?
qa.a: Sharmila felt resentful and disappointed, smiling politely while losing the sweets she had helped fry.

qa.q: What did Aai do that eased the evening for Sharmila?
qa.a: She noticed the sacrifice and had saved two gulab jamuns, rewarding Sharmila once the guests left.

qa.q: How might Aai feel when she flops onto the bed?
qa.a: Aai is probably tired and relieved, dropping the polite public face just as Sharmila can.

grounding: Shows a child made to sit properly and let guests eat first, missing a favourite sweet, and seeing the family's public and private faces.

passage:
Papa's new boss was coming to dinner, and the flat in Indiranagar had never been so clean.

"Ira, sit straight, say namaste, and don't talk about school fights," Mummy said. "And guests take the biryani first."

Ira sat. She watched Mr Rao take a second helping, then a third, until only rice and one lonely potato were left. That was her potato.

Her father, Nilesh, laughed at every one of Mr Rao's jokes, in a voice Ira had never heard before, deep and careful.

When the car finally pulled away, Nilesh collapsed on the sofa and loosened his tie. Ira stood in front of him and said, in the deep careful voice, "Ha ha, very good, sir."

Mummy snorted. Papa threw a cushion at her, laughing. "Okay, okay. Tomorrow I'll make you your own biryani."

qa.q: What was left after Mr Rao's third helping?
qa.a: Only rice and one lonely potato were left.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling as she watched Mr Rao eat?
qa.a: Ira felt resentful and annoyed at losing the biryani, and her potato, to the guest.

qa.q: How did Papa respond to Ira's teasing, and why did it help?
qa.a: He laughed and promised her own biryani tomorrow, acknowledging what she had given up.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt during dinner?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt nervous and careful, putting on a public voice to impress his new boss.

grounding: Shows a child told to behave and let a guest eat first, resenting the lost dish and noticing the family's public face versus its private one.

passage:
Afreen's board chemistry exam was at nine the next morning, and she and Avni were on a video call, halfway through organic reactions, when the doorbell rang. Khala, Khalu and four cousins, unannounced from Aligarh.

"Afreen, chai for everyone," Ammi called. "And the samosas from the freezer."

Afreen looked at her notes, then at her brother Saif, sprawled on the sofa with his phone. He had no exam. He didn't move.

"Why can't Saif make it?"

"Beta, he's a boy, he doesn't know how."

"Then he can learn tonight."

A small silence. Khala laughed. Ammi's cheeks went pink. Then she said, "Saif. Kitchen. Afreen will show you once, then she's going back to study."

Saif grumbled, but he poured the tea. Afreen was back on the call in eight minutes.

qa.q: How might Saif feel about being sent to the kitchen?
qa.a: Saif grumbled, perhaps embarrassed or put out, but he still poured the tea.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl pulled from exam study to serve surprise guests while her brother is left alone, and a fairer sharing of the serving.

passage:
Every Sunday it was the same. The bell would ring, a relative would appear at the Dadar flat, and Mummy would call, "Sarita, paani, chai!"

This Sunday Sarita was halfway through writing her debate speech for Monday. Kishore, her younger brother, was downstairs playing cricket.

She served Mama and Mami tea, then biscuits, then more tea, then washed the cups. Her speech lay on the bed, half a page long.

Mami said, "Such a good girl. Kishore is out?"

"Boys will be boys," Mummy laughed.

Sarita put the tray down harder than she meant to.

Papa noticed. After the guests left, he called down from the balcony. "Kishore! Up. Next Sunday you're on chai duty." Then, to Sarita: "Finish your speech. I'll wash these."

qa.q: What was Sarita writing when the relatives came?
qa.a: Sarita was writing her debate speech for Monday.

qa.q: What does Sarita putting the tray down hard suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt frustrated and resentful at serving all afternoon while Kishore played cricket and was excused as a boy.

qa.q: What did Papa do that made things fairer?
qa.a: He noticed, gave Kishore next Sunday's chai duty, and washed the cups himself so Sarita could finish her speech.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the afternoon?
qa.a: Mummy probably sees it as ordinary hospitality and a daughter's help, not noticing the unfairness in 'boys will be boys'.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl repeatedly pulled from study to serve relatives while her brother plays, and a parent correcting the unfairness.

passage:
"Ganga! Chai for Chachaji and Chachi!" Ma called.
Ganga looked up from her maths book. "Ma, I have a test tomorrow."
"Guests don't wait, beta."
"Lokesh has nothing tomorrow."
From the bed, Lokesh looked up from his comic. "Me? I don't know how to make chai."
"You make instant noodles every night," Ganga said.
"That's different."
"It's water and boiling. Same thing."
Ma stood in the doorway, hands on hips, looking from one to the other. "She has a point."
Lokesh groaned and rolled off the bed. "Fine. Ganga, how much sugar?"
"Two spoons for Chachaji. None for Chachi. And ask them how the drive was, don't just plonk it down."
"Yes, madam."
Ma laughed and went back to the guests. Ganga opened her book again, smiling.

qa.q: How much sugar does Chachaji take?
qa.a: Two spoons for Chachaji.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she pointed out that Lokesh has nothing tomorrow?
qa.a: Ganga felt frustrated at the unfairness of being pulled from test study while Lokesh was free.

qa.q: What made the solution work?
qa.a: Ma listened and agreed, and Lokesh took the chai duty, so the guests were still honoured and Ganga could study.

qa.q: How might Lokesh see being asked to make chai?
qa.a: Lokesh first resists, unsure of himself, but goes along with good humour once Ma backs Ganga.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl called away from study to serve guests while a sibling relaxes, and the serving being shared more fairly.

passage:
I share a flat in Pune with Farhan, so I saw the whole thing.

His cousin Gautam arrived on a Tuesday with one bag, "for two, three days", while he looked for work. By the second Monday he was still on our sofa, still looking.

Farhan kept smiling. He made extra rotis, lent his charger, and moved his study table to the balcony. But he started studying at the library till ten, and I noticed him checking the sofa before he came in.

On the twelfth night I heard them on the balcony. Farhan's voice was low. "Bhai, you're always welcome. But my exams start on the 20th. Can we find you a PG by Sunday? I'll help you look."

A long pause. Then Gautam said, "Sorry, yaar. I should have asked."

They went PG-hunting together on Saturday. I can't say what Farhan felt. He slept eleven hours on Sunday.

qa.q: How long did Gautam say he would stay?
qa.a: Gautam said "for two, three days".

qa.q: What might Farhan have been feeling behind his smile, and what hints at it?
qa.a: Farhan was probably stressed and tired, studying at the library till ten and checking the sofa before coming in, though the narrator can't know for sure.

qa.q: Why did Farhan's balcony talk work?
qa.a: He said his cousin was welcome, gave a real reason and a date, and offered to help find a PG, so the timing was honest and the bond stayed warm.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel after the balcony talk?
qa.a: Gautam seems embarrassed but not hurt; he apologises for not asking and goes PG-hunting with Farhan.

grounding: Shows a young host smiling through a relative's open-ended stay, and how a gentle, honest talk about timing protects both hospitality and the relationship.

passage:
Monday: Nirmala Bua arrived without warning, with two suitcases, for a wedding "somewhere near here". Sarita, twenty, gave up her room and smiled until her cheeks ached.

Friday: The wedding had been on Wednesday. Bua was still there, watching serials at full volume while Sarita tried to study for her semester exams on the kitchen floor. How long? Nobody would ask. You didn't ask Bua.

Next Tuesday: Sarita made Bua's favourite ginger tea and sat beside her. "Bua, I love having you. But my exams start Thursday and I'm studying on the floor. Could we plan your ticket for Wednesday? Come back after my exams, for longer."

Bua blinked, then laughed. "Arre, why didn't anyone tell me? I'm not a mind reader." She booked the ticket that evening.

qa.q: When had the wedding been?
qa.a: The wedding had been on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Sarita wondering as Bua stayed on, and how did she feel?
qa.a: Sarita kept wondering how long Bua would stay, feeling tired and stressed while studying on the kitchen floor but unable to ask.

qa.q: What made Sarita's talk with Bua work?
qa.a: She was warm first, gave a clear reason and a date, and invited Bua back for longer, so honesty didn't feel like rejection.

qa.q: How does Bua see the situation once told?
qa.a: Bua is surprised and a little amused, and wishes someone had told her sooner.

grounding: Shows a young host who smiles while wondering how long a relative will stay, and then gently raises timing in a way that keeps the relationship warm.

passage:
Sarika, you keep sighing at your phone. Your cousin is staying "one more week" again? Sit, and let old Tenzin tell you something.

When I was twenty, I rented one room above a shop in Kalimpong. My mother's cousin came from Sikkim "for a few days" to see a doctor. The few days became three weeks. I slept on the floor, smiled every morning, and wondered every night how long.

In our family you do not tell a guest to leave. So I said nothing, and started to dread going home.

My grandmother visited and saw my face. She said, "Silence is not kindness if it makes you bitter. Tell him the truth with a full plate in front of him."

So I cooked momos, and while he ate, I said, "Uncle, I'm so glad you came. My exams start next month; could you plan to go home by Sunday?"

He laughed at himself, and he still visits me every Losar.

qa.q: Where did Tenzin rent a room at twenty?
qa.a: Tenzin rented one room above a shop in Kalimpong.

qa.q: What was young Tenzin feeling during the three weeks?
qa.a: Tenzin felt tired and a growing dread about going home, smiling every morning while wondering every night how long.

qa.q: What turning point helped Tenzin speak up?
qa.a: The grandmother's advice that silence is not kindness if it breeds bitterness; Tenzin then gave a kind, clear date over a good meal.

qa.q: How did the uncle take being asked to plan his return?
qa.a: He laughed at himself and took no offence, and the bond stayed warm enough that he still visits every Losar.

grounding: Shows a young host who cannot say no to an overstaying relative, and how a gentle, honest word about timing protects both hospitality and the relationship.

passage:
Lavanya, before you go to your friend's house in Kochi, let your Manoj Mama tell you how I learned to be a guest.

At nineteen I went home with my hostel friend to his village for a weekend. I took nothing. I slept till nine, ate four times a day, and lay on their swing while his mother cooked for eight.

On Sunday I saw her sitting on the back step, rubbing her wrists. She looked so tired. I felt ashamed of myself.

So I washed every vessel in that kitchen, badly, while she laughed at me. And I caught the afternoon bus instead of the night one, so she could rest.

The next time I went, I took a box of Tirunelveli halwa and asked what I could chop. That family still calls me their second son.

A small gift, two hands in the kitchen, and leave before they're tired. That's all.

qa.q: What did Manoj take on his next visit?
qa.a: Manoj took a box of Tirunelveli halwa.

qa.q: What did Manoj feel seeing his friend's mother rubbing her wrists?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of himself for lying around while she cooked for eight.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Manoj visited?
qa.a: Seeing the tired mother on the back step; he washed the vessels and left early, and next time brought a gift and offered to chop.

qa.q: How might the friend's mother have felt when Manoj washed the vessels?
qa.a: She was amused and probably touched, laughing at his clumsy washing while getting some rest.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to be a good guest: bringing a small gift, helping in the kitchen, and leaving before the host is tired.

passage:
Disha had exactly four hundred rupees until the scholarship came, and Manjula Aunty had invited her for Sunday lunch in Chennai.

She couldn't buy a fancy sweets box. So on Saturday night, in the hostel pantry, she roasted besan and made a small jar of laddoos, slightly lopsided.

Aunty opened the door in a crumpled nurse's uniform. "Night shift," she yawned. "Come, come."

Disha put the jar in her hands and followed her into the kitchen. "What can I cut?" She chopped beans, stirred the rasam and laid the plates while Aunty sat down for once.

After lunch, Aunty's eyes kept closing mid-sentence. Disha stood up at three. "You sleep, Aunty. I'll come again soon."

At the door, Aunty held the lopsided jar to her chest. "These are better than shop ones."

qa.q: How much money did Disha have until the scholarship came?
qa.a: Disha had exactly four hundred rupees.

qa.q: Why did Disha stand up to leave at three?
qa.a: Disha felt caring and a little concerned; Aunty's eyes kept closing after the night shift, so she left to let her sleep.

qa.q: Which parts of Disha's visit made her a good guest?
qa.a: A small homemade gift, helping in the kitchen so Aunty could sit, and leaving before Aunty grew more tired.

qa.q: How does Manjula Aunty feel about the lopsided jar?
qa.a: Aunty is touched and grateful, holding it to her chest and saying the laddoos are better than shop ones.

grounding: Shows a young adult on a tight budget being a good guest with a homemade gift, help in the kitchen and an early goodbye.

passage:
For Christmas lunch, Elizabeth's family filled their Frazer Town flat with twenty-two people, and Pema was the only one who wasn't related.

She had brought a small packet of tea from her mother's garden in Sikkim, wrapped in newspaper and red ribbon. Elizabeth's grandmother sniffed it and smiled.

When the plates were cleared, Pema slipped into the kitchen and started drying dishes next to Elizabeth's aunt. "Guests don't wash!" the aunt protested. "I'm only drying," Pema said, and kept going.

At five she noticed the grandmother nodding in her chair and Elizabeth's mother leaning on the counter. Pema found her bag. "Thank you for having me. It was the best Christmas lunch I've had away from home."

Elizabeth walked her to the gate. "Amma says you're welcome any time. She never says that."

passage:
When Nadia and three old classmates flew into Seoul, Soo-ah booked the rooftop restaurant everyone posted photos of. She paid for all five dinners on her card before anyone could reach for a wallet.

She couldn't look poor. Not in front of the girls who remembered her family's tiny noodle stall.

At two in the morning she lay awake, doing sums on her phone. Rent was due in nine days.

On the last evening Nadia said, "Can we just stay in tonight? I want what your mum used to make us after school."

So Soo-ah made tteokbokki in her small kitchen, in her one good pot. They sat on the floor in socks until midnight, laughing about old teachers.

At the airport Nadia hugged her. "Last night was the best part of the whole trip."

qa.a: Rent was due in nine days.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling as she lay awake at two in the morning?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt anxious and afraid about the rent after overspending so she wouldn't look poor.

qa.q: What choice could Soo-ah make the next time she hosts?
qa.a: Choose a simple welcome at home, like the tteokbokki night, and if the spending has left her worried, talk it through with someone she trusts.

qa.q: How does Nadia experience the two kinds of evening?
qa.a: Nadia enjoyed the rooftop, but found the simple night in socks on the floor the best part of the trip.

grounding: Shows a host who overspends to avoid looking poor, anxious afterwards, and discovering that a warm, simple welcome is the real hospitality.

It was Gopika's turn to bring Friday snacks for the eleven staff at the bank branch, and last month Mrs Iyer had brought catered samosas and imported chocolates.

So Gopika ordered a full spread from the costly sweet shop, then a cake, then paneer rolls. She told herself it didn't matter. It was nearly a quarter of what she sent home each month.

At the staff table she watched faces while they ate, smiling too hard.

Mohit, the senior cashier, came over with his plate. "You didn't have to do all this."

"Everyone brings nice things."

"Everyone still remembers the poha you brought at Diwali," he said. "We asked Iyer ma'am for the recipe, and she said, ask Gopika."

Gopika laughed, and something in her chest loosened. Next month, she decided, it would be poha.

qa.a: There are eleven staff at the bank branch.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling as she watched faces at the staff table?
qa.a: Gopika felt anxious and eager to impress, smiling too hard and afraid of looking less generous than Mrs Iyer.

qa.q: What choice does Gopika make, and why is it a good one?

qa.q: How does Mohit see Gopika's spread?

grounding: Shows a young host spending beyond her means out of fear of judgement, and realising a simple, warm offering is still real hospitality.

passage:
Dear Francis,

You asked how Diwali went with Sameer's whole family visiting. Honestly? It looked perfect. New dinner set, four kinds of sweets, a caterer for the second night. Sameer's Bua said, "Such a grand welcome!" and I glowed.

What I didn't tell anyone: most of it went on my card. I kept thinking, if it's simple, they'll say we're struggling, that his wife can't manage.

Now the bill has come, and my stomach drops every time I see the envelope.

The funny thing? The moment everyone loved most was the second morning, when Sameer's Dadi and I sat on the balcony with plain chai and she told me stories about his childhood.

I've decided to tell Sameer everything tonight, look at it together, and talk to someone at the bank about it.

Next time, chai on the balcony.

Parul

qa.q: What did Sameer's Bua say about the welcome?
qa.a: Sameer's Bua said, "Such a grand welcome!"

qa.q: How does Parul feel when she sees the bill envelope?
qa.a: Parul feels anxious and afraid; her stomach drops, after spending so as not to look like she couldn't manage.

qa.q: What choice has Parul made about the bill?
qa.a: To tell Sameer everything, look at it together, and speak with someone at the bank, instead of hiding it.

qa.q: What did the balcony morning seem to mean to Sameer's Dadi?
qa.a: Dadi seemed to enjoy simply sitting with Parul over plain chai and sharing stories, which needed no expense.

grounding: Shows a young host who overspends on a grand welcome out of fear of judgement, and realises the simplest moment was the real hospitality.

passage:
Varun, you leave for Amsterdam next week, so let your Parveen Khala tell you about my first English tea.

I was twenty-four, a new nurse in Leeds, invited to my ward sister's house. She asked, "Would you like a cup of tea?" And I said, "No, no, please don't trouble," the way we do in Lucknow, waiting for her to insist twice.

She said, "Right-o," and poured one for herself.

I sat there for an hour, dying of thirst, too proud to ask. On the bus home I laughed until I cried.

The next week a friend from Glasgow explained: here, a no is a no. So at the next visit, when she asked, I said, "Yes, please, milk and one sugar." She smiled as if I'd given her a present.

And when she came to my flat, I insisted three times, and she looked terrified!

qa.q: Where was Parveen working at twenty-four?
qa.a: Parveen was a new nurse in Leeds.

qa.q: What did young Parveen feel sitting without tea for an hour?
qa.a: Parveen felt thirsty and embarrassed, too proud to ask after refusing the way she would in Lucknow.

qa.q: What turning point helped Parveen with English hospitality?
qa.a: A friend from Glasgow explaining that a no there is final, so the next time she simply said yes.

qa.q: How might the ward sister have felt when Parveen insisted three times at her flat?
qa.a: She probably felt confused and a bit alarmed, since where she came from one offer is enough.

grounding: Shows a young person discovering that one culture expects refusing and insisting while another takes a first no as final.

passage:
Damini had forty minutes to catch the last bus back to her flat in Amman, and Zainab's mother was not letting her leave.

"One more piece of knafeh!"

"No, thank you, I'm full."

The plate came anyway. Damini ate it. Then came the coffee. She drank one tiny cup; it was refilled at once. A second; refilled again. She glanced at the clock, panicking.

Zainab leaned over, laughing. "Shake the cup side to side when you're done. Otherwise my mother thinks you're just being polite."

Damini tilted the cup gently from side to side. Zainab's mother smiled, took it, and finally let her stand.

On the bus, Damini laughed to herself. At home in Nagpur she did exactly this to guests, insisting till they gave in. She had never once wondered how it felt from the other side.

qa.q: How long did Damini have to catch the last bus?
qa.a: Damini had forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling as her coffee cup kept being refilled?
qa.a: Damini felt panicked and a little embarrassed, full, watching the clock, and unsure how to refuse politely.

qa.q: What local rule helped Damini, and why?
qa.a: Shaking the cup side to side signals you're finished; knowing it let her decline without offending her host.

qa.q: How might Zainab's mother see Damini's first 'No, thank you'?
qa.a: She took it as polite modesty, not a real no, so she kept offering the way her custom expects.

grounding: Shows a young person abroad discovering a host who insists past a first refusal, and learning the local signal that avoids both offence and awkwardness.

passage:
Sumit had warned his mother that Ritu grew up in Hamburg, but Mummy still did what she always did.

"Take more rajma, beta."

"No, thank you, I'm fine," Ritu said.

Mummy heaped two more spoons on anyway. Ritu's smile froze, and she ate every grain.

Later it went the other way. Sumit's little cousin said no to Ritu's homemade biscuits, expecting her to insist. Ritu simply nodded and closed the tin. His cousin stared at it, crushed.

In the car Sumit laughed. "In my house the first no means nothing. The third no means maybe."

"In mine, no means no," Ritu said. "I was so full I couldn't breathe."

"Next time say, 'I'm really full, Aunty, it was lovely.' And my cousin will learn to say yes the first time."

qa.q: Where did Ritu grow up?
qa.a: Ritu grew up in Hamburg.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling as he watched the two mix-ups?
qa.a: Sumit was amused and sympathetic, laughing in the car as both his mother's and Ritu's rules misfired.

qa.q: What does Sumit suggest for next time?
qa.a: Ritu can say 'I'm really full, Aunty, it was lovely' so the no sounds final, and his cousin can learn to say yes the first time.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when Mummy heaped on more rajma?
qa.a: Ritu felt awkward and overfull; her smile froze, but she ate it all to be polite.

grounding: Shows a young person noticing that his family insists past a first no while a friend takes a first no as final, and how knowing the rule avoids awkwardness.

Snack-time note, KG-B, Wednesday — Kavitha

Pankaj (5) has started saying "Jootha!" about everything. Today Aarohi held out half her sandwich to him, a big bite missing, and he jumped back as if it were hot. "No! Jootha!"

Aarohi's lip wobbled. She thought he meant she was dirty.

I asked Pankaj what jootha means. "Something bad. Mummy says don't take it." He didn't know why; he only knew the rule.

"Nahi, beti," Dadi said, gently catching her wrist. "For God, only what nobody has bitten. That one is jootha."

Nandini looked at the guava, then at Yusuf, puzzled. "But it's still good."

"Good for you two. For God, we give fresh." Dadi took a whole guava from her bag, and Nandini placed it very carefully.

Abhinav, you laughed at Rishabh's tiffin today because it had no onion? Come here. Let your Gargi Nani tell you about Mitali.

When I was nine in Kolkata, I went to my friend Mitali's house for the first time. In our Jain home there were no eggs, no onions, nothing from under the ground. In her kitchen, a whole fish lay on the chopping board, eyes and all.

I said, "Chhi! You eat that?"

Mitali's face fell. Her mother came in and didn't scold me. She said, "Your house cooks one way, ours another. Would you like to help me make luchi?"

I stood beside her and asked a hundred questions, kindly this time.

Mitali and I stayed friends for sixty years. That "Chhi" is the one word I would take back.

qa.q: What lay on the chopping board in Mitali's kitchen?
qa.a: A whole fish lay on the chopping board, eyes and all.

qa.q: How does Gargi feel now about her 'Chhi'?
qa.a: Gargi deeply regrets it; it is the one word she would take back, because it hurt Mitali.

qa.q: What turning point changed how young Gargi reacted to Mitali's kitchen?
qa.a: Mitali's mother calmly explained that each house cooks its own way and invited her to help with luchi, so kind questions replaced mocking.

qa.q: How did Mitali feel when Gargi said 'Chhi'?
qa.a: Mitali felt hurt and embarrassed; her face fell at the insult to her family's food.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a friend's home has different kitchen rules, mocking at first, and learning that asking kindly keeps the friendship open.

Tarun

Okay, I'm Sunaina, and this episode of Lunchbox Stories is about curd rice.

When we moved from Madurai to Delhi in Class 8, my mother packed curd rice with lime pickle every day. Some girls called it baby food. One boy called me Idli for a whole term. I started eating in the library corridor so nobody would see.

Then Pallavi, who sat behind me, found me there. She sat down, took a spoon, and said, "This is the best thing I've eaten in weeks. Why are you hiding it?"

I didn't have an answer.

The next day she brought her rajma-chawal and we swapped halves. Soon four people were swapping. Now there's a whole lunch table that fights over Amma's pickle.

So yes, it's the same curd rice. What changed was who was sitting with me.

qa.a: Sunaina felt ashamed and lonely, hiding in the library corridor after being called Idli and hearing the food called baby food.

qa.a: She sat with Sunaina, praised the food honestly and started swapping lunches, turning a hidden dish into a shared one.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have been thinking when she found Sunaina in the corridor?
qa.a: Pallavi probably felt puzzled and a little sad that such good food was being hidden, and wanted Sunaina to feel welcome.
